transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-02-03
Start: 15:00 PT
Duration approx: 52 minutes
Attendees: Alex Morales (Redwood AE), Priya Nair (Redwood SE), Mark Zhou (Helix Infra), Lea Torres (Helix ML Platform), Samir Patel (Helix CTO)

Auto-summary: See summary field.

[00:00:05] Alex (AE): hey everyone, thanks for joining. quick agenda — kernel handoff behavior we saw on your NVLink cluster, cudagraph replay flakiness, and kv-cache warmup impact on latency. priya's gonna drive the perf parts.

[00:00:28] Priya (SE): yeah hi, good to be here. i pulled together two repro traces you sent and ran a couple of baseline benches on a replica of your 8x A100 setup. note — some of the names in the trace got munged, so i might say "tensor r-t l-l-m" when i mean TensorRT-LLM, and "vee-ell-ell-em" for vLLM, apologies if that sounds odd.

[00:00:48] Mark (Helix): no worries. we've been seeing periodic tail spikes around 95th/99th when the kv cache evicts a shard and when cudagraph replays hit a new execpath. it's fairly consistent during peak sim load.

[00:01:05] Priya (SE): ok, so two likely culprits: one is kernel routing changes when the sequence-length distribution changes (short requests -> different kernel kernels), and two is cudagraph replay hitting a non-deterministic kernel path after quantized ops get fused. In our tests, TRT-LLM tends to pick specialized fused attention kernels more aggressively, while vLLM stays on a more conservative matmul path unless you force the kernel.

[00:01:35] Lea (Helix): when you say "force the kernel" what knobs are those? we tried autodetect settings but didn't find a stable combination.

[00:01:45] Priya (SE): good question. there's a couple: (a) set a sequence-length bucket for the route so the runtime picks the short-seq kernels, (b) disable certain cuda-graph optimizations during warmup, (c) pin quantization ABI to a compatible path so fused ops remain stable. i'll share the checklist.

[00:02:06] Samir (Helix): are these changes invasive? we run in a VPC with NFS-backed weight mounts on-prem, plus a swarm of preprocessing pods. any change that increases mount chatter is a hard no.

[00:02:20] Alex (AE): noted. part of pilot scoping will cover filesystem and network topology. priya, do we have data on NFS impact?

[00:02:30] Priya (SE): yes — in our reproducible bench we saw that model shard page faults that trigger disk reads can add 40-120ms depending on NFS latency. if your KV cache is persistent but shards are evicted due to memory pressure, the first tokens post-eviction show those tails. so it's both kernel and io.

[00:02:52] [00:03:05] Mark (Helix): hmm we do have intermittent memory pressure during background ETL spikes, which correlates. what's the best practice — reserve more GPU mem for kv cache or reduce batch size?

[00:03:18] Priya (SE): usually a combination: increase persistent KV cache footprint for hot prefixes, and enable eviction-aware batching — smaller latency-sensitive lanes for low-latency traffic, bigger for throughput. Redwood's autoscaler can pin a portion of memory to KV. i'll show config snippet.

[00:03:38] [00:03:50] Priya (SE): about cudagraphs — we saw this pattern: when cudagraph capture includes quant-fused ops, replay sometimes selects a different kernel if the graph was captured at a different device occupancy. TRT-LLM's graph replay is more tolerant because it has a fallback kernel table, but it's not magic. vLLM's non-cudagraph matmul path can be more stable at the cost of some throughput.

[00:04:12] Lea (Helix): i remember one of your docs mentioned "graph replay vs capture" — is capture deterministic across restarts? we saw different kernel ids on cold starts.

[00:04:22] Priya (SE): capture determinism depends on a couple of things: identical allocator state, same batching mix, same CUDA driver. slight divergence in async prefetch timing or allocator fragmentation can change which kernel the graph references. where possible we recommend a controlled warmup runner that simulates production sequences to populate the persistent cache and capture graphs under representative occupancy.

[00:04:45] [00:05:00] Mark (Helix): got it. what about quantization level — we've seen int8 slightly worse on some tasks. should we avoid quant for production?

[00:05:09] Priya (SE): quantization is workload dependent. For many instruction-following models int8 with per-channel scaling is fine, but for dense retrieval retraining or reranking tasks, FP16 or mixed precision sometimes preserves the top-k ordering better. For latency-sensitive endpoints, we often recommend a hybrid: use int8 for the bulk, but keep a FP16 fallback route for high-precision queries. that's what Redwood's routing policy can do.

[00:05:40] [00:05:55] Samir (Helix): the hybrid route sounds promising. how do you measure regression risk? we've had subtle rank flips that are hard to detect until user complaints.

[00:06:05] Priya (SE): we tie quality checks to prompt sets. you keep a small corpus of golden prompts and evaluate output similarity metrics (embedding cosine, normalized edit distance) on every rollout. Redwood Optimize can automate alerts when the metric drifts beyond your threshold. we'll include an example config in the docs link.

[00:06:25] [00:06:40] Alex (AE): can we dive into a concrete timeline for the pilot resources? Mark, what's your capacity for a dedicated pilot cluster?

[00:06:50] Mark (Helix): we can spare a 4x A100 rack for a two-week pilot initially. it's behind our internal VPC with strict egress rules and a corporate KMS. we need to ensure no plaintext model artifacts leave the subnet.

[00:07:09] Priya (SE): that's fine. Redwood Private supports a control plane that can operate over an HSM-backed KMS and reference architecture for on-prem. for the pilot we'll ask for a set of sample traces, ssh access to a bastion for ops, and a small NFS snapshot. we'll avoid moving raw weights out; we'll pull metrics via Prometheus and CUPTI/NVPROF captures you produce.

[00:07:36] [00:07:50] Lea (Helix): about kernel handoff: can you clarify what you mean by "tiebreaker" heuristics? how does runtime decide between a fused attention kernel and a fallback matmul kernel?

[00:07:58] Priya (SE): runtime uses a cost model based on sequence length, batch size, and occupancy; if two kernels have similar estimated cost but one has lower tail variance we sometimes pick the one with lower worst-case. in TRT-LLM there's an additional lookup table tuned for A100 memory layout that biases toward fused kernels when the KV cache is warm. the tiebreaker can be influenced by occupancy and quant ABI. the problem is when occupancy changes mid-flight — cudagraph replay baked at different occupancy can point to a kernel that's not optimal, causing latency spikes.

[00:08:36] [00:08:50] Mark (Helix): are there runtime flags to prefer stability over throughput at the cost of 5-10% perf? we prefer predictable p99 over occasional bursts.

[00:08:58] Priya (SE): yes — there's a "stability-first" profile we can enable: it disables certain kernel fusions at capture time, enforces a fixed kernel table, and increases KV cache reservation. throughput drops 4-12% depending on model, but p99 improves substantially.

[00:09:18] [00:09:30] Samir (Helix): what's the operational burden of that profile? do we need to re-bench every model version?

[00:09:36] Priya (SE): minimal — we recommend a lightweight bench on deploy which takes ~10-15 minutes to validate the profile on a pinned sample. For major model changes we run the fuller bench suite. Redwood's toolchain automates the bench and pushes the results to the console for review.

[00:09:58] [00:10:15] Alex (AE): for our action items, we'll send the kernel checklist and a sample config. Priya, anything else to call out?

[00:10:22] Priya (SE): yes a couple of pragmatic notes from the lab: (1) avoid mixed NFS mounts for pageable shards — use in-memory or a.local SSD when possible, (2) capture cudagraphs after warmup under production traffic, not during cold start, (3) prefer per-route sequence bucketing so short and long requests don't collide in the same graph, and (4) keep a FP16 fallback route in case int8 mis-orders critical ops. i'll paste these as bullet items in the shared note.

[00:10:55] [00:11:10] Mark (Helix): about traces — i'll pull a 30-minute run that includes ETL spikes. what format is most useful? nvprof? cup ti? what about the Redwood perf dashboard?

[00:11:20] Priya (SE): NVPROF/CUPTI flame graphs are ideal. include CUDA kernel ids, timestamps, and a sample of the first 1s after shard eviction. CSV with kernel durations is fine too. we ingest into our perf dashboard (link: https://console.redwood.ai/pilot/helix-rtk) — i'll send access.

[00:11:40] [00:11:55] Samir (Helix): one last security thing: we need SOC2/ISO artifacts and a list of what telemetry Redwood collects during pilot.

[00:12:05] Alex (AE): we'll attach SOC2 and ISO summaries to the pilot doc; telemetry is metric-only by default, traces only if you opt-in and push. no PII or raw user data will be collected unless you enable it. we'll send the policy.

[00:12:20] Priya (SE): also practical debug tip — when you see a tail spike, capture a short cudagraph replay and a device memory map snapshot. often it shows a new allocator offset that changes kernel selection. we linked a sample memory-map screenshot in the shared doc.

[00:12:40] [00:12:55] Mark (Helix): ok that resonates. quick question on benchmarking: you mentioned TRT-LLM performed better but had more volatile kernels; vLLM was steadier. any numbers you can share from your lab run?

[00:13:08] Priya (SE): on our reproduced Helix workload: throughput (tokens/sec) TRT-LLM = 1.18x vLLM when fully warmed; median latencies comparable, but p99 TRT-LLM was 1.5-2x vLLM in cases with eviction events. with stabilization profile enabled, TRT-LLM p99 matched vLLM while still giving ~1.05x throughput. i'll attach the CSV.

[00:13:40] [00:13:55] Lea (Helix): interesting. so pilot recommendation is to run both stack variants side-by-side? that seems heavy but may be worth it for comparison data.

[00:14:05] Priya (SE): yes — a canary approach: route a small percentage (5-10%) to TRT-LLM with stability profile off to measure throughput, and route production traffic to the more stable path or to a hybrid route. Redwood Console can do A/B and rollback automatically.

[00:14:25] [00:14:40] Alex (AE): let's capture next steps — priya to share kernel-checklist and console links, mark to upload traces, alex to send pilot scope and price sketch, schedule pilot kickoff week of 2027-02-15. any objections?

[00:14:55] Mark (Helix): none. thank you.

[00:15:00] Samir (Helix): thank you, this was useful.

[00:15:05] Alex (AE): cool. we'll follow up in email with the links and sprint tasks. thanks all.

(End of transcription — remaining time used for side chat not captured.)
